# Joseph and Aseneth — Reader's Guide
**Guide:** HESED | **Category:** Pseudepigrapha (PS)

---

## At a Glance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Attribution** | Anonymous |
| **Actual Composition** | c. 1st century BCE to 2nd century CE (debated; possibly late 1st century BCE or early 1st century CE) |
| **Language** | Greek (multiple recensions — a longer and a shorter form with significant differences) |
| **Audience** | Probably Jewish readers interested in the theology of conversion; possibly Diaspora Jewish communities; later, Christian communities |
| **Genre** | Hellenistic romance; conversion narrative; mystical/liturgical fiction |
| **Length** | 29 chapters in two parts |
| **In One Sentence** | Aseneth, an Egyptian noblewoman of extraordinary beauty and pride, is shattered by her encounter with Joseph's divine radiance, undergoes a week of solitary penance, receives a heavenly visitor who feeds her the honey of immortality, and emerges as a transformed "City of Refuge" — and then must survive a murderous plot that tests whether the mercy she has received can become the mercy she gives. |

---

## Sections Overview

### Part One: Aseneth's Conversion (Chapters 1–17)

#### 1. Aseneth's Introduction and Joseph's Arrival (Chapters 1–6)
Aseneth is introduced as a young woman of extraordinary beauty — but also arrogance. She has rejected all suitors, including the son of Pharaoh, and lives in a high tower surrounded by seven virgin companions. When Joseph arrives at her father Pentephres' estate during the grain distribution, Aseneth sees him from her high window and is initially contemptuous: she will not marry a foreign slave. Then she sees his face.

Joseph's face shines. He is described in divine-warrior and royal terms: his robe is white and gold, his face is like the sun, his eyes are like sunlight, his cheeks like fields of pomegranate, his hair like a bunch of grapes. He is explicitly "a son of God." Aseneth is undone. She recants her contempt immediately, confesses she spoke foolishly, and falls into anguished longing.

Joseph, for his part, refuses to kiss Aseneth — she worships idols and is therefore not his sister in faith. He prays for her: "Lord, bless this young woman and renew her by your spirit, and may she eat your bread of life and drink your cup of blessing and number her among your people."

#### 2. Aseneth's Penance (Chapters 9–13)
After Joseph's departure (he promises to return in eight days), Aseneth goes to her high tower and begins a week of devastated penance. She strips off her rich clothing, puts on a black mourning robe, removes her jewelry, throws her idols from the window, and pours her feasting food out to the dogs — for it has been offered to idols and is polluted. She sits in ashes and weeps.

Her lament is extensive and theologically rich: she confesses her arrogance, her idolatry, her rejection of the living God, and her worthlessness. She compares herself to an orphan who has no one to run to. She fears that the God of Joseph will not receive her because her lips have been "polluted" by the food of idol-worship.

#### 3. The Heavenly Visitor and the Honeycomb (Chapters 14–17)
On the eighth day, as Aseneth is finishing her lament, a figure appears — a man whose appearance exactly replicates Joseph's: shining face, sparkling garments, a staff. But this figure is an angel, possibly the archangel Michael (the name is never given in the text). He addresses her as "Aseneth" and calls her "blessed" — and tells her that God has heard her penance and her name has been written in the book of the living.

The angel then commands that food be brought. A honeycomb appears — white as snow, full of honey that smells like myrrh. The angel breaks off a piece and places it in Aseneth's mouth: "Eat." This is the honey of incorruption from the bees of Paradise, the food of the angels, and by eating it Aseneth will receive immortal life and be renewed entirely.

The angel then reveals her new names and identity: she will be called "City of Refuge" (*polis kataphyge*), for in her all the nations who convert to God will take refuge. She is to receive Joseph as her husband.

The angel departs. Aseneth emerges from her tower transformed — her mourning robe replaced, her face shining "like the sun." When Joseph returns and sees her, he takes her in his arms: now she is his sister.

---

### Part Two: The Plot Against Joseph (Chapters 18–29)

#### 4. The Marriage and Simeon and Levi (Chapters 18–21)
Aseneth and Joseph marry. Pharaoh himself officiates at the wedding, marveling at Aseneth's beauty. The couple has two sons: Manasseh and Ephraim. This part of the narrative is brief — the conversion story was the main event.

#### 5. The Plot (Chapters 22–29)
Pharaoh's son, still furious at being rejected by Aseneth, conspires with Simeon and Levi's brothers (Dan, Gad, Naphtali, and Asher) to kidnap Aseneth and kill Joseph. Simeon and Levi refuse to participate. The plot is set in motion: an ambush on Aseneth's litter.

Aseneth survives through miraculous protection, the conspirators' weapons turn against themselves, and Benjamin — the youngest brother, who accompanies Aseneth — fights heroically. When the conspirators are disarmed and kneeling before Aseneth, she intercedes for them: she will not allow them to be killed. This act of forgiveness — mercy extended to the people who just tried to murder her — is the text's final theological statement. Aseneth the convert has become Aseneth the embodiment of the mercy of God.

Pharaoh's son dies from the wound Benjamin gave him. Pharaoh himself dies of grief shortly after. Joseph becomes regent of Egypt for forty-eight years.

---

## The World Behind the Text

Genesis 41:45 provides the entire textual hook for this long narrative: "Pharaoh called Joseph's name Zaphnath-Paaneah, and he gave him Aseneth the daughter of Potiphera priest of On as his wife." That is all Genesis says. For ancient readers, this created a problem: How could Joseph — the paradigmatically righteous man of the patriarchal narratives — have married an Egyptian woman, the daughter of a pagan priest? How was the integrity of the Israelite lineage preserved?

The *Joseph and Aseneth* narrative resolves this problem: Aseneth converted. Genuinely, wholly, and at enormous personal cost. She is not a Gentile wife accepted through a convenient fiction; she is a transformed human being whose conversion is so complete that she becomes the prototype and patron of all future converts.

The text was almost certainly composed in a Diaspora Jewish context in which conversion to Judaism — and the social and theological questions surrounding it — was a live issue. The Hellenistic world produced many conversions; Jewish communities needed a theology of what conversion meant and what it accomplished.

The two recensions of the text (a longer and a shorter version) differ significantly enough that some scholars treat them as distinct works or distinct stages of editorial development. The longer text is more mystical, more liturgical, and more theologically elaborate; the shorter text is more narrative-focused. The question of which is "original" is unresolved.

---

## Why This Book Was Written

**1. To solve a narrative problem.** Genesis provides no account of Aseneth's background or character. This text provides both — in a way that makes the marriage theologically unimpeachable.

**2. To articulate a theology of conversion.** What does it mean to convert to the God of Israel? The text's answer is comprehensive: it means abandoning idolatry completely (physical destruction of idols, rejection of idol-food), genuine and extended penitential grief, divine encounter and transformation, reception of heavenly food (a ritual initiation), and the conferral of a new identity and name. Conversion is not intellectual assent — it is death and rebirth.

**3. To establish the dignity of converts.** By making Aseneth not merely a convert but the "City of Refuge" — the prototype and patron of all who come to God from the nations — the text assigns to converts a place of honor in sacred history. The convert Aseneth is not a lesser Israelite; she is the model for what Israel's God is doing in the world.

**4. To explore the female interior life.** This is one of the only ancient texts of any kind in which a woman's subjective experience — her shame, her grief, her transformation, her courage — is the central subject of the narrative. The extended lament scenes in chapters 11–13 are among the most psychologically detailed portraits of spiritual crisis in ancient literature.

---

## How to Read This Book

**Read Part One slowly; Part Two is almost a different book.** The conversion narrative (chapters 1–17) is the literary and theological heart of the text. Part Two (chapters 18–29) reads more like an adventure story and feels less carefully crafted. Some scholars suspect Part Two was added later or drawn from a separate source. Do not judge the whole by the adventure plot.

**Pay close attention to the honeycomb scene (chapters 16–17).** This is the mystical center of the text. The honey is described with extraordinary elaboration: it came from bees that "fed on the dew of heaven" in Paradise, it is the food by which angels are sustained, and its consumption transforms Aseneth from a mortal to someone who will never die. This is not merely symbolic eating — it is initiation into a new ontological status. Whether you read it as a ritual (baptism, eucharist, or Jewish proselyte immersion with a meal), as mystical transformation, or as the food of the world to come, the scene repays sustained attention.

**Notice the visual parallels between Joseph and the angel.** The angel's appearance is described in the same terms as Joseph's in chapter 5. This is not an accident. The text is suggesting that what Aseneth saw in Joseph's face — the divine radiance — was the divine itself; that Joseph is a transparently divine figure whose presence already initiated her transformation. The angel completes what Joseph's face began.

**Track how Aseneth changes.** In chapter 4 she is contemptuous and haughty. In chapter 11 she is shattered. In chapters 14–17 she is remade. In chapter 29 she is the agent of mercy toward her would-be murderers. The arc is the theological claim: this is what conversion does to a person.

---

## The Threads — How This Book Connects

### With Genesis
- **Genesis 41:45** is the sole canonical hook — Joseph married Aseneth daughter of Potiphera.
- **Genesis 41:46–57** (Joseph's administration of Egypt) provides the background for Part One.
- The names **Manasseh and Ephraim** (Genesis 41:51–52) appear in chapter 21 as the children of Joseph and Aseneth.
- Aseneth's penance — stripping off rich clothes, sitting in ashes, seven days of fasting — echoes the mourning rituals of the Hebrew Bible (Job 2, Jonah 3).

### With the Song of Songs
- The description of Joseph in chapters 5–6 (his cheeks like pomegranate, his eyes bright, his hair like grapes) draws directly on the erotic poetry of the Song of Songs. This is the language of the beloved. Joseph is the divine beloved who draws the soul toward transformation.
- Aseneth's seven virgins parallel the "daughters of Jerusalem" who accompany the female speaker in the Song.

### With the New Testament
- The **"bread of life," "cup of blessing," and eating-and-drinking language** in Joseph's prayer for Aseneth (chapter 8) resonates with Johannine eucharistic and wisdom themes (John 6) and with 1 Corinthians 10:16. Whether there is direct dependence or shared tradition is debated.
- The **"new creation" language** — Aseneth is to be renewed by God's spirit, made into a new creature — parallels 2 Corinthians 5:17 ("if anyone is in Christ, new creation") and Galatians 6:15.
- The **"City of Refuge" title** given to Aseneth has no direct NT parallel but resonates with the NT imagery of the church as a gathered community of the redeemed, and with Hebrews 6:18 (believers who "flee for refuge" to God's promise).
- Aseneth's **forgiveness of her enemies** (chapters 28–29) parallels the Sermon on the Mount ethic and the forgiveness scenes of the Joseph story in Genesis 50.

### With Jewish Proselyte Tradition
- The text reflects and possibly prescribes a **theology of proselytism**. The physical destruction of idols, the extended mourning, the reception into the community, the new name — these elements correspond to what later rabbinic literature describes as the process of conversion (renunciation, immersion, sacrifice, and new identity).

### With Philo of Alexandria
- Philo's allegorical interpretation of the Aseneth tradition in *On Dreams* treats Aseneth as the soul that is redeemed and united with Joseph (the figure of divine order). The *Joseph and Aseneth* narrative may share a tradition with Philo's allegorical framework, or may be the narrative expression of the same symbolic reading.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

1. **"City of Refuge" is a loaded title.** In the Torah, the **cities of refuge** (Numbers 35) were designated cities where a person who had accidentally caused a death could flee from the avenger and be safe until trial. Calling Aseneth by this title makes her a living embodiment of the divine provision for the vulnerable and the guilty. She does not just receive mercy — she *becomes* the place where mercy is found. This is among the most beautiful and theologically precise images in the text.

2. **The pollen-dew-honeycomb chain is a mystical cosmology.** The text explains that the bees of Paradise fed on the dew of heaven (= divine sustenance), made their honey from that dew, and the honey therefore transmits divine life to those who eat it. This is not primitive biology — it is a careful chain of transmission from heaven to earth to Aseneth's mouth. The honey is sacramental in a precise sense: a material substance that carries divine reality.

3. **Joseph's refusal to kiss Aseneth in chapter 8 is not coldness — it is holiness.** He refuses because she worships idols and her mouth has been defiled by idol-food. This is the same logic that underlies later rabbinic concerns about shared meals with Gentiles. Joseph's restraint is not rejection; it is the establishment of the terms under which union with the holy is possible. After her conversion, the kiss happens.

4. **The seven virgins are liturgically significant.** Aseneth has exactly seven virgin companions — the same number as the seven days of penance, the seven heavens, and the seven spirits who appear in the angel scene. The number seven throughout the text signals completeness, holiness, and the divine order of creation.

5. **The text is unusual in the ancient world for centering on female interiority.** Ancient literature generally depicts women from the outside — their beauty, their actions, their effects on men. The *Joseph and Aseneth* narrative spends chapters in Aseneth's inner world: her shame, her grief, her dialogue with herself and with God. This is not incidental to the genre — it is the genre. The conversion of a soul is an interior event, and the text insists on following that event inward.

6. **The shorter and longer recensions disagree on significant details.** The shorter recension (arguably earlier) omits some of the more elaborate mystical elements and the full "City of Refuge" typology. Readers encountering different translations may notice these differences. Neither recension has been established as definitively original.

---

## Why This Book Isn't in Your Bible

*Joseph and Aseneth* was never a candidate for inclusion in the Hebrew Bible or in any Jewish canon: it is an expansion of a two-word biblical reference, not a prophetic or legal text. It circulated as devotional and entertaining religious literature.

In the Christian tradition, the text was read and copied — it survives in numerous Greek manuscripts, as well as in Syriac, Armenian, Latin, Slavonic, and Ethiopian versions, suggesting wide and sustained readership. But it was not treated as scripture; it was treated as edifying narrative, closer to hagiography than to canonical text.

Its exclusion from Christian canons reflects its genre (romance, not prophecy or law), its pseudonymous authorship (Aristeas never existed as the named narrator; the text has no named author), and its late date.

Its value for modern readers — especially for understanding conversion theology, Second Temple Jewish narrative imagination, and the role of women in ancient religious literature — is independent of its canonical status. It is one of the most beautiful and theologically rich texts in the pseudepigraphal corpus.

---

## Timeline

| Date (approx.) | Event |
|---|---|
| c. 1st century BCE – 2nd century CE | Range of proposed composition dates; most scholars favor c. 100 BCE – 115 CE |
| c. 1st century CE | Philo of Alexandria's allegorical treatment of Aseneth in *On Dreams* |
| c. 2nd–4th century CE | Text in circulation in Jewish and Christian communities; translated into Syriac and other languages |
| c. 5th–7th century CE | Armenian, Slavonic, and Latin versions appear |
| 1889 CE | P. Batiffol's first critical edition of the Greek text |
| 1983 CE | C. Burchard's translation in *The Old Testament Pseudepigrapha* (Charlesworth, vol. 2); still the standard English translation |
| 1996 CE | Ross Shepard Kraemer publishes *When Aseneth Met Joseph* — major feminist and historical reassessment |
| 2005 CE | Randall Chesnutt and others continue to debate date, provenance, and the Jewish vs. Christian origin question |

---

*HESED notes: This guide was written for readers encountering Joseph and Aseneth for the first time. The conversion narrative in chapters 1–17 is among the most sustained and psychologically sophisticated accounts of spiritual transformation in ancient literature. Readers who come to it expecting a simple romance will find something considerably stranger and more demanding — a text that insists the meeting with the holy is shattering before it is healing, and that the person who emerges from that meeting is genuinely new.*
